sources.outlet: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs
sources.quote: to resolve allegations that it knowingly submitted false claims to Medicare and Medicaid arising from medically unnecessary inpatient hospital admissions, a kickback and physician self-referral scheme and the use of erroneous diagnosis codes.
sources.searcher_note: $10.25M False Claims Act settlement: unnecessary inpatient admissions, admission-volume bonuses to doctors, false SIRS diagnosis codes. Live page bot-walled; Wayback copy 2025-02-04 has the quote. Also at justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/...

sources.outlet: U.S. Department of Justice, settlement agreement (U.S. ex rel. Guardiola and Fisher v. Oroville Hospital)
sources.quote: Oroville Hospital knowingly submitted to Medicare and Medi-Cal claims that included false diagnosis codes for systemic inflammatory response syndrome
sources.searcher_note: Covered conduct: false SIRS secondary codes (ICD-10 R65.10) Jan 2013-Jul 2023, and medically unnecessary inpatient admissions Jan 2014-Jul 2023. Note SIRS R65.10 is non-infectious SIRS, not a sepsis code as such. Date is the announcement date; the PDF itself was not dated in the extracted text.

sources.quote: The settlement additionally resolves allegations that Oroville Hospital admitted patients as inpatients when it knew inpatient care was not medically necessary.
sources.searcher_note: Local news on the settlement: kickbacks tied to admissions, false SIRS claims, unnecessary inpatient admissions; also carries the hospital's denial. Same-day rewrites by Action News Now, Becker's, KQMS count as copies.

sources.quote: Oroville Hospital makes no admissions of wrongdoing, maintaining that it would have prevailed if the case was decided on a level playing field and categorically denying any violation of the law.
sources.searcher_note: Disagreement: the hospital denies the admissions and coding allegations; says disputes began in 2019 and CEO says related cases were disproved.

sources.outlet: Arnold & Porter, FCA Qui Notes blog (Meredith Osborn)
sources.quote: Oroville Hospital allegedly submitted claims to Medicare and Medi-Cal knowing the claims included a fabricated secondary diagnosis code, allowing the hospital to claim excessive reimbursement for illusory
sources.searcher_note: Law-firm analysis: DOJ contends the conduct ran January 2013 to July 2023; relator Cecilia Guardiola filed in 2020 (Case No. 2:20-CV-1558, E.D. Cal.).

notes: Same entity and same direction found (unnecessary inpatient admissions, diagnosis-code upcoding), but no source states 1.78 stays per patient, the 2,109-hospital ranking, the 3,938 stays / 2,213 patients, or a sepsis share (30% vs 15% CA median). The coding allegation is about SIRS (R65.10) secondary codes, not sepsis DRGs; the judge should weigh whether that is the same finding. Post-cutoff coverage found (Press Democrat 2026-08-10, Action News Now: hospital sues ex-CEO Robert Wentz over a property self-dealing scheme) is unrelated to admissions or coding; not recorded. The search tool's summary of query 7 attributed a 2026 OIG audit ($12.1M overpayments, 26 of 100 claims) to Oroville; checking the OIG page shows that audit is Sarasota Memorial Hospital, not Oroville. Not recorded.
